questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between a classical random walk and a quantum walk?
options: A quantum walk only ever moves in one fixed direction, never randomly
A quantum walk uses a classical coin flip but a quantum position register, with no other differences
A quantum walk evolves via unitary, interference-based dynamics, staying in superposition across paths until measured, instead of collapsing to a definite direction at each probabilistic step
There is no meaningful difference; the two produce identical statistics on any graph
questions.explain: The classical walk collapses probabilistically at each step; the quantum walk's coin-plus-shift evolution stays coherent, letting paths interfere with each other, which is the source of its different spreading behavior.

questions.q: In the discrete-time coin-plus-shift construction, what do the coin register and shift operator each do?
options: Both operators act only on the coin register and never touch the position register

The coin register is put into a superposition of directions by a coin-flip operator; the shift operator then moves the position register in each direction conditioned on the coin, entangling the two registers
The coin register stores the final answer; the shift operator measures it immediately
The shift operator decides the coin's state; the coin register has no effect on position
questions.explain: Each step applies a coin-flip operator (creating superposition over directions) followed by a shift operator (moving position conditioned on, and entangled with, the coin), repeated step after step to build up interference.

questions.q: How does quantum walk spreading on a line compare to classical random walk spreading, in big-O terms?
options: Both spread identically as O(sqrt(t)), with no difference
Classical random walks spread faster, as O(t), while quantum walks spread as O(sqrt(t))
Quantum walks spread ballistically as O(t); classical random walks spread diffusively as O(sqrt(t)) -- a quadratic speedup in spreading and hitting time
Quantum walks spread as O(t^2), an exponential improvement over classical O(sqrt(t))
questions.explain: Quantum walks spread linearly in the number of steps (O(t)) due to coherent interference, versus the classical diffusive O(sqrt(t)), giving a quadratic speedup in reaching a given distance or node.

questions.q: What is the explicit connection between Grover's algorithm and quantum walks described in this lesson?
options: Grover's algorithm and quantum walks solve completely unrelated problems with no shared mathematical structure
Quantum walks were derived by directly simplifying Shor's algorithm, with no connection to Grover's

Grover's algorithm can itself be reformulated as a specific instance of a quantum walk search on a particular graph, reproducing Grover's sqrt(N) scaling exactly -- showing it's one case of a broader quadratic-speedup family
Grover's algorithm is strictly faster than any quantum walk search, with no equivalence between them
questions.explain: Grover's algorithm is a specific case of quantum walk search -- a walk on a graph built from the search space whose coin-and-shift dynamics reproduce amplitude amplification's quadratic speedup, generalizing it to broader graph-search settings.

questions.q: Why does the quadratic speedup of quantum walks place them in the same speedup family as Grover's algorithm rather than Simon's algorithm?
options: There is no real distinction between quadratic and exponential speedups; both terms describe the same kind of gap
Quantum walks actually provide an exponential speedup, identical to Simon's algorithm's gap
Quantum walks and Simon's algorithm both solve hidden-subgroup problems, unlike Grover's algorithm

Quantum walks and Grover's algorithm both provide a quadratic (polynomial-degree) gap over their classical counterparts, while Simon's algorithm provides a proven exponential gap -- a qualitatively different, unbounded-growth separation
questions.explain: A quadratic speedup (quantum walks, Grover's) scales the classical cost down by a fixed power (square root); an exponential speedup (Simon's) creates a gap that grows without bound as the problem size n increases -- these are fundamentally different categories of advantage.
